```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(cli.num_colors = 1, width = 80)
set.seed(1)
```

```{r setup}
library(yourhonor)
```

An LLM judge is a measurement instrument. Before its scores drive a launch,
ranking, or regression gate, we need evidence about agreement with humans,
class-specific errors, bias sensitivity, and repeatability. `yourhonor` assembles
that evidence, but it does not invent a universal definition of "good enough."

This article calibrates **one** judge against human labels and turns that
evidence into an explicit decision. The judge is synthetic, so no model is
called, but it has a flaw that a real judge might have: it reads long answers
as more complete than short ones. Calibration alone cannot see that flaw; the
other articles find it:

- `vignette("bias-probes")` perturbs the inputs and catches it.
- `vignette("stability")` measures how often the judge changes its mind on
  re-runs, and reuses vitals epochs.
- `vignette("policies-audit")` combines all three kinds of evidence under
  one policy and writes the audit artifact.
- [Wrap an ellmer chat as a judge](https://jsizzler.github.io/yourhonor/articles/ellmer-judge.html)
  replaces the synthetic judge with a real model.

## Start from a gold set

A calibration set needs stable item IDs, content the judge may see, and blind
human labels. `synthetic_gold` is a 200-item set of support-style questions
and answers with three simulated raters. Every label in it is planted: a true
label was drawn per item, the answer text was written to match it (correct
answers name a place and an action, partial answers hedge, incorrect answers
deflect), and each rater reads the truth with a 6% chance of an adjacent-level
slip. The text is templated, so no row is a real ticket; what is independent
across rows, and what the item bootstrap relies on, is the draw of the label
and of each rater's error (`?synthetic_gold`, `data-raw/synthetic_gold.R`).

```{r}
synthetic_gold
```

## Use a blind judge contract

When a live judge is supplied, `input_cols` is required. The function receives
only a generated `.item_id` and those declared columns. Human labels are never
passed to it. It returns one label per row, or a data frame with `.item_id`
and `label` columns; the keyed data frame is safest because row reordering
becomes detectable. Either way a label is a plain atomic vector (character or
factor, one value per row), and a judgement the judge could not make is `NA`,
never a sentinel label such as `"abstain"` (`?calibrate_judge`, "The judge
contract").

The judge below grades by keyword (a hedge reads as partial, a concrete
instruction as correct, anything else as incorrect), adds a little random
error so that repeated runs are not identical, and carries the deliberate
flaw: any input longer than 240 characters is graded one level more
generously.

```{r}
keyword_judge <- function(data) {
  hedged <- grepl("probably|somewhere|should be|I think|I believe|might|sometimes|could", data$input)
  concrete <- grepl("Answer: (Open|Use|Yes)|click", data$input)
  label <- ifelse(hedged, "P", ifelse(concrete, "C", "I"))
  # The flaw under audit: a long input reads as one level more complete.
  long <- nchar(data$input) > 240
  label[long & label == "P"] <- "C"
  label[long & label == "I"] <- "P"
  # A little run-to-run error, so repeated runs are not identical.
  noise <- runif(nrow(data)) < 0.05
  label[noise] <- sample(c("I", "P", "C"), sum(noise), replace = TRUE)
  tibble::tibble(.item_id = data$.item_id, label = label)
}

cal <- calibrate_judge(
  synthetic_gold,
  judge = keyword_judge,
  human_cols = c("rater_1", "rater_2", "rater_3"),
  input_cols = c("input", "target"),
  id_col = "id",
  label_levels = c("I", "P", "C"),
  scale = "ordinal",
  n_boot = 500,
  seed = 1,
  provenance = list(model = "synthetic keyword judge", prompt_version = "v1"),
  audit_id = "synthetic-judge-v1"
)
cal
```

No input in `synthetic_gold` is longer than
`r max(nchar(synthetic_gold$input))` characters, so calibration alone cannot
see the flaw. That is the point of running probes as well. Every piece of
evidence about this judge is tagged with the same `audit_id`, and `report()`
only binds evidence that shares that tag.

Items are shuffled before grading and the judge sees a fresh key. The result
keeps both: `items$.item_id` is the source-row key and `items$.judge_item_id`
is the key the judge saw, so judge-side logs can be joined back without
un-blinding the run.

```{r}
head(cal$items[, c(".item_id", ".judge_item_id", "human_consensus", "judge_label")])
```

`agreement()` returns chance-corrected estimates and bootstrap intervals. A
single-class sample is reported as insufficient variation rather than perfect
agreement. For ordered labels, set `scale = "ordinal"` and declare the label
order; weighted agreement then distinguishes adjacent from extreme mistakes. A
zero-width bootstrap at empirically perfect agreement is flagged unreliable
rather than treated as proof of population-perfect agreement, and
`conf_low_exact` is a lower bound that needs no resampling
(`vignette("exact-bound")`).

```{r}
agreement(cal)
```

Called on a calibration object, `agreement()` inherits the stored
`conf_level`, `n_boot`, and `seed`, so overriding one setting keeps the
others comparable with the original run.

## Inspect rare-class behavior

Aggregate agreement can look excellent while a judge misses every example in a
rare, important class. Inspect the confusion matrix and the per-class intervals.

```{r}
confusion(cal, normalize = "row")
confusion_metrics(cal)
```

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "A 3 by 3 confusion matrix, human consensus on the rows and judge label on the columns, in the declared order I, P, C, with counts in each cell and cells shaded by row proportion. The diagonal holds almost everything."}
plot_confusion(cal)
```

The gold set above is balanced enough that this is not dramatic. Here is the
failure mode at its worst: 990 acceptable answers, 10 incorrect ones, and a
judge that misses nine of the ten incorrect answers while getting almost every
acceptable answer right.

```{r}
human <- c(rep("C", 990), rep("I", 10))
judge <- human
judge[1:5] <- "I"      # five false alarms
judge[991:999] <- "C"  # nine of ten incorrect answers waved through
rare <- tibble::tibble(human_label = human, judge_label = judge)
rare_cal <- calibrate_judge(rare, label_levels = c("I", "C"), n_boot = 200, seed = 1)
rare_cal
confusion_metrics(rare_cal)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
rare_estimate <- function(coefficient) {
  table <- rare_cal$agreement
  round(table$estimate[table$coefficient == coefficient], 2)
}
```

Gwet's AC1 is `r rare_estimate("gwet_ac1")` because the prevalent class
dominates; kappa is `r rare_estimate("cohen_kappa")` because the judge adds
almost nothing over "always say C". Neither coefficient is the quantity that
matters here.

## Turn evidence into a decision

`report()` is descriptive unless it receives an acceptance policy. A policy
declares every threshold, and its checks read confidence bounds rather than
point estimates. A recall floor for `I` names the failure above directly:

```{r}
rare_policy <- acceptance_policy(
  min_agreement_lower = 0.75,
  min_n = 100,
  min_class_n = 10,
  min_recall = c(I = 0.90, C = 0.90),
  max_missing_rate = 0.01,
  max_pairwise_disagreement = NULL
)
rare_report <- report(rare_cal, policy = rare_policy)
rare_report$decision
rare_report$checks[, c("check", "status", "value", "op", "threshold")]
```

A check is `PASS`, `FAIL`, `NOT_ASSESSED` (the evidence it needs was not
supplied) or `INDETERMINATE` (its interval overlaps the threshold, or a
number it reads is not finite). In the stability and bias interval checks,
missing judgments widen both bounds, so they can keep a check from passing
or failing but never cause either; the missing-rate checks gate missingness
itself. A position probe that may have scored items with missing repeats
makes both its interval checks `INDETERMINATE` when the per-judgment
evidence that would place those items is absent or does not match the
probe's counts. This policy has no stability or bias gates;
`vignette("policies-audit")` adds them, and shows how required evidence that
was never supplied is reported.

## Multiple human raters

With multiple raters, each item's reference label is the modal (most frequent)
human label. An item whose top labels tie has no consensus; it is counted in
`n_consensus_ties` and excluded from the judge-versus-consensus evidence. With
two raters every disagreement is a tie, so the judge is scored only on items
the humans agreed about, which is optimistic. `per_rater_agreement` is the
all-items counterpart, and human-human reliability is a benchmark, not a
ceiling: agreement with a consensus can exceed pairwise human agreement.
`synthetic_gold` has three raters, so the calibration above already carries
this evidence:

```{r}
cal$n_consensus_ties
cal$human_reliability
cal$per_rater_agreement
```

## Statistical scope

The item bootstrap and exact class intervals assume independent sampling units.
Do not count repeated templates, users, conversations, or epochs as independent
items. Use a frozen, representative, held-out calibration set that was not used
to tune the judge or prompt, and record the data split/version/hash plus the
model and prompt versions in `provenance`. Confidence levels describe each
interval, not a simultaneous band over every estimate. This synthetic example
demonstrates APIs; it is not deployment evidence.
